title: The LORD Will Provide on Moriah
summary: God tests Abraham by asking for Isaac; Abraham obeys in faith, God supplies a ram in Isaac’s stead, and swears to bless all nations.
historicalContext: Genesis 22 belongs to the later years of Abraham’s life, after the birth of Isaac, the departure of Ishmael, and the covenant with Abimelech at Beer-sheba, where Abraham had settled on the edge of the Negev. Isaac has grown into a young man able to carry a load of wood up a mountain. The journey to “the land of Moriah” takes three days northward into the hill country later occupied by Jerusalem, a site Scripture itself identifies with the temple mount (2 Chronicles 3:1). Among the surrounding peoples, offering a firstborn child to a deity was known as an extreme act of devotion, and Israel’s later law would condemn it as an abomination. The chapter closes with news from Nahor’s family in Mesopotamia, preparing for the search for Isaac’s bride in chapter 24 and linking Abraham’s household with relatives who had remained in Haran.
literaryContext: This chapter is the summit of the Abraham narrative that opened with the call of Genesis 12. The command “get thee” deliberately repeats the wording of that first call, so that Abraham’s life is framed by two acts of costly obedience: leaving his past and surrendering his future. The narrator discloses in the first verse that the event is a test, then tells it in spare, tense prose driven by verbs and by repeated words—“father,” “son,” “together,” “here am I”—and by the key verb “see,” which also means “provide.” The father–son dialogue at the centre (vv. 7–8) carries the theological weight. Speeches from heaven reverse the original command, reveal a substitute, and seal the promises with an oath, the last recorded word of God to Abraham. The genealogy of Nahor (vv. 20–24) then turns toward the next generation by introducing Rebekah, answering the genealogy of Terah that stood before Abraham’s call (11:27–32).
themes: God’s testing of a faith He intends to strengthen
Obedience that trusts God with the future
Substitution: a ram in the stead of the son
The LORD who sees and provides
The sworn promise of blessing to all nations

outline.title: The Test Announced
outline.summary: God calls Abraham and commands him to offer Isaac, his only and beloved son, as a burnt offering in the land of Moriah.

outline.title: The Journey of Faith
outline.summary: Abraham sets out at once, leaves the servants with a promise to return, and answers Isaac’s question with the confession that God will provide the lamb.

outline.title: The Altar and the Substitute
outline.summary: Abraham binds Isaac on the altar, the Angel of the LORD stays his hand, a ram is offered in Isaac’s stead, and the place is named The LORD will provide.

outline.title: The Oath of Blessing
outline.summary: The LORD swears by Himself to multiply Abraham’s seed, give it victory, and bless all nations through it; Abraham returns to Beer-sheba.

outline.title: News from Nahor’s House
outline.summary: A report of Nahor’s twelve sons introduces Rebekah, preparing the way for Isaac’s marriage and the continuation of the promised line.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass after these things, that God did tempt Abraham, and said unto him, Abraham: and he said, Behold, here I am.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“After these things” ties the scene to everything that has gone before: the long delay of the promised son, the laughter at Isaac’s birth, the painful dismissal of Ishmael, and the settled years near Beer-sheba with which chapter 21 closes. Enough time has passed for Isaac to have grown from a weaned child into a young man able to climb a mountain under a load of wood. Then the narrator does something unusual: he tells the reader the meaning of the event before it begins. “God did tempt Abraham.” Abraham himself is not told; the reader is, so that no one will imagine that the God of Abraham hungers for the blood of children.

The English word “tempt” has narrowed in meaning since 1611. Here it means to test or prove. Scripture insists that God entices no one to evil (James 1:13); what He does is bring His servants into circumstances that reveal and strengthen what is in their hearts (Deuteronomy 8:2). Moses would later tell trembling Israel at Sinai that God had come “to prove you,” so that His fear would keep them from sin (Exodus 20:20). Divine testing belongs inside the covenant relationship. It is the work of a Father who intends to bless.

God calls the patriarch by name, and Abraham answers with a single Hebrew word, “Here I am.” The exchange is brief and familiar. Over many years Abraham has learned to recognize the voice that called him out of Ur and Haran, and his answer expresses readiness before he knows what will be asked. The same reply will sound again when Isaac speaks to him (v. 7) and when the Angel of the LORD calls from heaven (v. 11), marking the three movements of the story.

This is the climactic trial of Abraham’s life. Earlier tests concerned leaving his past; this one concerns surrendering his future. A faith that has grown slowly through failures and recoveries is now asked to stand at full height.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to put to the proof, to try the quality of something or someone. When God is the subject, it describes His testing of His people’s loyalty, as with Israel in the wilderness and at Sinai. When people are the subject and God the object, it describes presumptuous unbelief that demands He act on their terms. Modern translations rightly render it “tested” here, since the English “tempt” now suggests enticement to sin, which God never does.

A single word formed from “behold” with the first-person suffix. It is the answer of a servant ready to hear and obey, used by Moses at the bush, Samuel in the temple, and Isaiah in his vision. In this chapter Abraham speaks it three times—to God, to Isaac, and to the Angel of the LORD—showing the same attentive readiness throughout the ordeal.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God’s command comes in three imperatives: take, go, offer. Between them the description of Isaac tightens like a cord: “thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest.” Each phrase narrows the focus and raises the cost. Ishmael still lived, but he had been sent away, and God had declared that “in Isaac shall thy seed be called” (Genesis 21:12). Isaac was the only son of the promise, the one through whom every word about descendants, land, and blessing to the nations was to be fulfilled. This is also the first time Scripture uses the verb “love,” and it is spoken of a father’s love for his son. The God who commands knows exactly what He is asking.

“Get thee” renders the same Hebrew expression with which Abraham’s journey began (Genesis 12:1). The first call asked him to give up his country, his kindred, and his father’s house; the last asks him to give up the son in whom his future lay. In both, the destination is left partly undisclosed: a land that God would show him, and now “one of the mountains which I will tell thee of.” Obedience has to begin before every detail is known.

The land of Moriah appears again only in 2 Chronicles 3:1, where Solomon builds the temple “in mount Moriah” on the threshing floor David purchased after the destroying angel’s hand was stayed over Jerusalem. The link is deliberate. The hills to which Abraham was sent would become the place where Israel’s sacrifices were offered for centuries, and close by, outside the city wall, the Son of God would die.

“Offer him there for a burnt offering” is the hardest phrase in the chapter. The burnt offering was consumed entirely on the altar, a sacrifice of total dedication. Child sacrifice was practised among the peoples of Canaan, and the law would later condemn it as an abomination (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31; Jeremiah 19:5). The story itself answers the moral question: the reader already knows this is a test, and the climax will show God forbidding the deed and supplying a substitute. Abraham, however, does not know the end. The command seems to contradict the promise, and he must trust that the God who gave Isaac by miracle can be trusted with Isaac’s life.

Abraham makes no reply. The man who pleaded at length for Sodom says nothing here. His answer will be given in the morning by what he does.

wordNotes.explanation: The adjective yachid means only, unique, solitary. Isaac was not Abraham’s only offspring, but he was the only son of Sarah and the sole heir of the covenant promise, which makes him unique in God’s purpose. The Greek Old Testament renders the word here as “beloved” (agapētos), the very term the Father uses of Jesus at His baptism and transfiguration. Hebrews 11:17 calls Isaac Abraham’s “only begotten,” the description John applies to Christ.

The name comes from a verb meaning to go up, since the whole offering ascended to God in smoke. Unlike other sacrifices, no part was kept back for the worshipper or the priest; everything was given. It expressed complete dedication and, in the later law, made atonement for the worshipper. The term heightens the totality of what God asks of Abraham here.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham rose up early in the morning, and saddled his ass, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son, and clave the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and went unto the place of which God had told him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrative moves quickly through a chain of plain verbs: he rose early, saddled, took, clave, rose up, went. No feelings are described and no words are spoken, yet the restraint of the telling makes the weight of each act felt. Abraham rises “early in the morning,” as he had when he sent Hagar and Ishmael away (Genesis 21:14). He does not delay, argue, or seek advice. Whatever he endured during the night, the morning finds him obedient.

The order of the preparations is striking. Saddling the animal and choosing two young servants are the ordinary tasks of any journey. Splitting the wood is mentioned last, as if it were the task he could put off longest. Every stroke of the axe readied the fire on which his son was to be laid. Abraham could not be sure that suitable fuel would be found at the unnamed mountain, so he carried it with him from Beer-sheba.

Sarah is not mentioned. The text does not say whether she knew, and it is wise not to fill the silence with speculation. The narrative keeps attention on Abraham and on one question: will he trust God’s word when it seems to undo God’s promise?

The verse ends with Abraham going “unto the place of which God had told him.” His direction comes from God alone. Long before, he had set out “not knowing whither he went” (Hebrews 11:8). Now he sets out knowing all too well what awaits him at the end of the road, and he goes.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb describes rising at dawn to begin a task, and in Genesis it often marks prompt response to a word from God or a decisive situation. Abraham rose early after interceding for Sodom and again when he sent Hagar away. Here it shows obedience that does not linger over the hardest command he ever received.

The intensive form of a verb meaning to split or break open. Abraham split the wood himself instead of leaving the work to his servants. Its position at the end of the list of preparations lets the reader feel what this task meant for a father who knew what the wood was for.

verses.bibleText: Then on the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes, and saw the place afar off.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The journey from Beer-sheba to the hill country of Jerusalem covers roughly fifty miles, a natural distance for a laden donkey and travellers on foot to cover in two full days and part of a third. The detail fits the location named in verse 2 and anchors the account in real geography.

The three days also gave Abraham time. A rash act done in a moment of fervour would prove little. Three days of walking beside his son, with every step bringing the mountain nearer, showed whether his resolve rested on settled trust. The text records no wavering. When Abraham “lifted up his eyes, and saw the place afar off,” he recognized it as the place God had appointed. God had promised to show him the mountain (v. 2), and He did. The same faithfulness that guided each step of the way now marks out its end.

The sight of the place “afar off” must have been a hard moment. Distance had allowed the destination to remain somewhat abstract; now it stood before him on the horizon. Yet seeing the goal did not turn Abraham back. Faith does not require that the road ahead look easy; it requires that the One who appointed the road be trusted.

In Scripture the third day often marks a turning point of deliverance (Exodus 19:11; Hosea 6:2; Jonah 1:17). For Abraham it brought him to the place where he would receive his son back, as it were, from death (Hebrews 11:19). The pattern finds its fulfilment when Christ rose from the grave “the third day according to the scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:4).

wordNotes.term: בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי (bayyom hashshelishi) — on the third day
wordNotes.explanation: A common biblical time marker that often introduces a decisive moment after a period of waiting or preparation, such as the LORD’s descent on Sinai or Esther’s approach to the king. Here it measures the length of Abraham’s trial and anticipates the third-day deliverance that runs through Scripture to the resurrection of Jesus.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham said unto his young men, Abide ye here with the ass; and I and the lad will go yonder and worship, and come again to you.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
At the foot of the mountain Abraham leaves the servants and the donkey behind. What lies ahead is not for spectators. Father and son will go up alone, and the solitude of the climb matches the solitude of the faith being tested; no one else could carry this decision for him.

Abraham names the purpose of the ascent: “I and the lad will go yonder and worship.” The word for worship means to bow down in reverence before God. Abraham does not describe the act he dreads as a tragedy or a loss. He calls it worship, the yielding to God of what God has a right to ask.

Then comes the remarkable promise: “and come again to you.” The verbs are plural—we will go, we will worship, we will return. Abraham was not deceiving the servants. Hebrews 11:17–19 explains what he believed: he reasoned that God was able to raise Isaac even from the dead. God had said that Abraham’s seed would be called through Isaac (Genesis 21:12), and God had now commanded Isaac’s death. Abraham held both words together. He did not expect to be spared the sacrifice; he expected God to keep His promise on the far side of it. Paul describes the same faith when he speaks of Abraham believing in the God “who quickeneth the dead” (Romans 4:17).

Isaac is called “the lad” (na‘ar), a term that can describe a young man of marriageable age or one fit for service. He is no small child. The servants are also “young men,” the same word, which suggests that Isaac was of comparable strength. Whatever happens on the mountain will not be forced on a helpless infant.

wordNotes.term: וְנִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה וְנָשׁוּבָה (wenishtachaweh wenashuvah) — and worship, and come again
wordNotes.explanation: Both verbs are first-person plural with a cohortative sense: “let us worship and let us return.” The first describes bowing low in reverent homage before God. The second states Abraham’s expectation that he and Isaac would both come back. Read with Hebrews 11:19, the wording expresses resurrection faith rather than a polite cover for his intention.

The word covers a wide span of age, from infancy to young adulthood. It describes Joseph at seventeen, Shechem when he sought a wife, and young men serving as attendants or soldiers. Since Isaac is able to carry the wood up the mountain, the context points to a young man rather than a child.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering, and laid it upon Isaac his son; and he took the fire in his hand, and a knife; and they went both of them together.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham lays the wood on Isaac and carries the fire and the knife himself. The division of the load is natural—the young man takes the heavy bundle, the father the dangerous implements—yet the picture is unforgettable. Isaac climbs the hill bearing the wood intended for his own sacrifice. Centuries later Jesus would go out “bearing his cross” to the place of a skull (John 19:17). The parallel arises from the larger pattern of Scripture, in which the beloved son carries up the hill the instrument of his own death.

The fire was probably carried as live coals in a vessel, since kindling a flame on the mountain could not be counted on. The word for knife is uncommon and is used of a blade for cutting up flesh (Judges 19:29; Proverbs 30:14). Abraham holds in his hands the very things he must use against his son.

“They went both of them together.” The phrase will return at the end of verse 8, framing the dialogue between father and son. It describes companionship, a shared walk without hostility or fear. Whatever Isaac sensed, he walked beside his father, and whatever Abraham suffered, he walked beside his son. The narrator lets the silence speak.

In the larger story of Scripture, the Father and the Son moved toward Calvary in perfect unity of purpose (John 10:17–18). Abraham’s journey offers a faint human reflection of what it cost God to give His only Son.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun is related to the verb “to eat” and describes a knife for cutting meat. It occurs only rarely, for the blade the Levite used in Judges 19 and, figuratively, for the devouring teeth of oppressors in Proverbs 30. Its use here underlines the grim reality of what Abraham carried.

The adverb means in unity, side by side. Repeated in verses 6 and 8, it encloses the only conversation between Abraham and Isaac and emphasizes their shared journey. A form of the same expression returns in verse 19 when the whole company goes home together.

verses.bibleText: And Isaac spake unto Abraham his father, and said, My father: and he said, Here am I, my son. And he said, Behold the fire and the wood: but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The silence breaks with a single word, “My father.” It is the only time Isaac speaks in the chapter. Abraham answers as he had answered God at the beginning: “Here am I, my son.” The readiness he offered God, he offers his son. The words “father” and “son” recur again and again in the chapter, keeping the cost before the reader.

Isaac’s question is logical and innocent: “Behold the fire and the wood: but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?” He knows how sacrifice is done. He has watched his father build altars and offer animals. Everything needed is present except the victim. The question is the hinge of the narrative, because only God can answer it.

It also reaches far beyond Moriah. From the skins with which God clothed Adam and Eve (Genesis 3:21) to Abel’s firstlings (Genesis 4:4) and Noah’s altar after the flood (Genesis 8:20), sacrifice had taught that sin brings death and that God accepts a substitute. Yet the blood of animals could never finally take away sin (Hebrews 10:4). Through the long centuries of Israel’s altars, Isaac’s question remained open: where is the lamb? John the Baptist gave the answer at the Jordan: “Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world” (John 1:29).

wordNotes.explanation: A simple term of address that carries the affection and trust of a son. Placed beside Abraham’s reply, “my son,” it frames the exchange in family intimacy and makes the pathos of the moment unmistakable. The same address will later be spoken by Esau and Jacob to the aged Isaac.

Seh is a general word for one animal of the flock, whether sheep or goat, young or full-grown. It is the term used for the Passover victim in Exodus 12 and for the sheep led to slaughter in Isaiah 53. Isaac asks for “the” seh, the expected victim; God will provide a ram, and in the end His own Son.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham said, My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering: so they went both of them together.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham’s answer is the theological centre of the chapter: “My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering.” In the Hebrew, “God” stands first for emphasis. Supplying the sacrifice rests with God alone. Abraham cannot produce it; he can only trust that God will.

The verb translated “provide” is the ordinary word “to see.” To see to something is to attend to it and supply what is needed, much as English speaks of “seeing to” a matter. The theme of seeing runs through the chapter. Abraham “saw the place afar off” (v. 4); he will lift up his eyes and see the ram (v. 13); he will name the place “The LORD will see” (v. 14). God sees the need before His servant does, and seeing, He provides. Hagar had already learned that He is the God who sees (Genesis 16:13).

Abraham may have chosen his words with tenderness, answering Isaac without yet telling him all. Yet they were more than a gentle evasion. They expressed faith, and they proved truer than Abraham could have known. God did provide, first a ram caught in the thicket and, in the fullness of time, His own Son. “Provide himself a lamb” can be read “provide for himself,” meaning that the offering is of God’s own choosing and belongs to Him. The Lamb God would finally provide was taken from no human flock; He was the Son who came from the Father’s bosom (John 1:18), “foreordained before the foundation of the world” (1 Peter 1:19–20).

Here the typology of the chapter comes into full view. Isaac, the only and beloved son, is spared, and a substitute dies in his place. Christ, the only and beloved Son of the Father, is not spared but given “for us all” (Romans 8:32), so that sinners under sentence of death may live. Abraham’s statement thus became a prophecy of Calvary, the substitutionary sacrifice in which God Himself supplied what humanity could never offer. Jesus may have had this scene in mind when He said, “Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad” (John 8:56).

The verse closes as verse 6 did: “so they went both of them together.” Whether Isaac grasped his father’s meaning is not stated. What is clear is that he kept walking, and the trust that would let him be bound on the altar is already visible in his willingness to go on beside his father.

wordNotes.term: אֱלֹהִים יִרְאֶה־לּוֹ הַשֶּׂה (Elohim yir’eh-lo hasseh) — God will provide himself a lamb
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “God will see for himself the lamb.” The verb ra’ah, “see,” here carries the sense of looking out for and supplying, as when the LORD says to Samuel, “I have provided me a king.” The fronted subject stresses that God, and no one else, will do it. The phrase anticipates the place-name of verse 14 and, in the light of the New Testament, the Lamb whom God appointed for the world’s redemption.

verses.bibleText: And they came to the place which God had told him of; and Abraham built an altar there, and laid the wood in order, and bound Isaac his son, and laid him on the altar upon the wood.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The pace slows as father and son reach the summit. Each step of the preparation is listed: Abraham built an altar, laid the wood in order, bound Isaac, laid him on the altar upon the wood. These are the actions of a man resolved to obey to the end. “Laid the wood in order” uses language later found in the sacrificial law, where the priests arrange the wood upon the fire (Leviticus 1:7).

Abraham had built altars before—at Shechem, near Bethel, at Hebron (Genesis 12:7–8; 13:18)—marking the land with worship. This altar is different. On it he places the son of the promise in place of a lamb from the flock.

The binding of Isaac gave the chapter its traditional Jewish name, the ‘Aqedah. Isaac was a young man; his father was well over a hundred. Isaac could have resisted or fled. That he allowed himself to be bound indicates that Abraham had told him what God required and that Isaac yielded. His submission makes him a fitting picture of the Son of God, who prayed, “not as I will, but as thou wilt” (Matthew 26:39), and of the Servant who “is brought as a lamb to the slaughter” and “openeth not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7).

The faith of Abraham and the trust of Isaac meet on this altar. One gives what he loves most; the other surrenders his life into his father’s hands. Both rely on God, whose purpose they cannot yet see. Paul would later urge believers to present their bodies “a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1). Isaac on the wood, still breathing, is an early and vivid picture of that self-surrender.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb ‘aqad, to bind hand and foot, occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible, though a related adjective describes Jacob’s streaked flocks. Later Jewish usage applied it to tying the lamb of the daily offering, and the noun ‘aqedah, “binding,” became the name for this whole chapter. The rarity of the word sets the moment apart.

The verb means to arrange or set in proper order, used for setting a table, drawing up a battle line, and arranging the wood and the pieces of a sacrifice on the altar. It shows that Abraham prepared the offering with deliberate care, as worship.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham stretched forth his hand, and took the knife to slay his son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrative reaches its most dreadful moment in the fewest words. Abraham “stretched forth his hand, and took the knife to slay his son.” The verb “slay” is the word used for slaughtering sacrificial animals (Leviticus 1:5, 11). Nothing is softened. Abraham’s obedience is complete in intention; only the stroke remains.

The faith tested here is not presumption. Abraham did not choose this act for himself, and he did not do it to win God’s favour by a spectacular offering. He acted because God had commanded it, trusting that the God of the promise would remain faithful even through death. Hebrews describes the moment as an offering already made: “By faith Abraham, when he was tried, offered up Isaac” (Hebrews 11:17). In will and purpose the sacrifice was complete. The tense of that verb in Hebrews treats the offering as an accomplished act, even though Isaac never died.

James points to the same scene as proof that Abraham’s faith was alive. His trust in God was shown to be real by what he did (James 2:21–22). Faith and obedience stand together here: the obedience grows out of the faith and makes it visible to God and to all who read the account.

wordNotes.explanation: Shachat is the technical verb for slaughtering an animal in sacrifice, regularly used in Leviticus for killing the offering before the LORD. Its use with “his son” as the object shocks the reader and shows that Abraham was prepared to carry out the command as an actual offering.

verses.bibleText: And the angel of the LORD called unto him out of heaven, and said, Abraham, Abraham: and he said, Here am I.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
At the decisive instant heaven speaks. “The angel of the LORD called unto him out of heaven.” Until now the narrative has spoken of “God” (Elohim). Here the covenant name, the LORD, appears with the messenger who intervenes. The Angel of the LORD in Genesis speaks and acts as God Himself. He promised Hagar that He would multiply her seed (Genesis 16:10), and in verse 16 He will swear “by myself… saith the LORD.” He is distinguished from the LORD and yet identified with Him. These features point to the pre-incarnate Son of God, the “messenger of the covenant” (Malachi 3:1), who stays the hand raised against Isaac long before He offers Himself for the world.

The double call, “Abraham, Abraham,” conveys urgency. Similar doubled names appear when God calls Jacob, Moses, Samuel, and Saul of Tarsus at turning points in their lives (Genesis 46:2; Exodus 3:4; 1 Samuel 3:10; Acts 9:4). The knife is already lifted; the voice must reach Abraham at once.

Abraham answers for the third time, “Here am I.” The word he spoke to God in the night and to Isaac on the slope he speaks now with the knife in his hand. His readiness has not changed through the ordeal. He is as willing to stop at God’s word as he was to begin at it, which shows that his act was obedience to God and not a will of his own driving him onward.

wordNotes.term: מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה (mal’akh YHWH) — the angel of the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: Mal’akh means messenger, one sent. Yet the Angel of the LORD speaks in the first person as God, receives the reverence due to God, and is identified with the LORD by those who meet Him. At the burning bush the Angel appears and the LORD speaks from the flame. Hosea calls the One who wrestled with Jacob both an angel and the LORD God of hosts. These patterns point to a divine Person who is sent by the Father, best understood as the pre-incarnate Christ.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Lay not thine hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him: for now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The command is emphatic and doubled: “Lay not thine hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him.” God forbids the act and forbids any harm at all. The scene that began with a command to offer Isaac ends with a command to spare him. The God who tested Abraham makes plain that He does not want the death of the son. Human sacrifice, which the surrounding nations practised, is rejected on the very mountain where Israel would later worship (Deuteronomy 12:31; Jeremiah 7:31).

“For now I know that thou fearest God.” God does not need experiments to discover what is in a human heart; He searches every heart (Psalm 139:1–4). The statement means that Abraham’s fear of God has now been displayed in history, in an act that God, Abraham, Isaac, and every later reader can see. To fear God in Scripture is to hold Him in reverent trust and to order one’s life by His word. Abraham’s fear of God was proved by the fact that he held nothing back.

“Thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me.” The words of verse 2 return, and God names again the cost of what Abraham was willing to give. The Greek Old Testament renders “withheld” with a verb meaning “spare,” and Paul takes up that very language in Romans 8:32: God “spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all.” What God stopped Abraham from doing, God Himself did. Abraham’s son was spared; the Father’s Son was not.

This verse also shows that God counted Abraham’s offering as made. He looked at the surrendered heart and accepted it (Hebrews 11:17). The value of the sacrifice lay in a will yielded wholly to Him, for, as Samuel would later say, “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22). And it was precisely because Abraham did not withhold his son that he received him back.

wordNotes.term: יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים (yere’ Elohim) — thou fearest God
wordNotes.explanation: The fear of God in the Old Testament is reverent awe that issues in trust and obedience. It is the beginning of wisdom and the mark of the righteous, such as Job and the midwives of Egypt. Abraham had earlier assumed that there was no fear of God in Gerar; now his own fear of God is openly demonstrated.

wordNotes.term: וְלֹא חָשַׂכְתָּ (welo’ chasakhta) — thou hast not withheld
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to hold back or keep for oneself. Joseph uses it when he says Potiphar had withheld nothing from him. The Greek Old Testament translates it here with pheidomai, “to spare,” the verb Paul uses of the Father who “spared not his own Son.” The echo shows that the apostle read Genesis 22 as a portrait of God’s gift in Christ.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and behold behind him a ram caught in a thicket by his horns: and Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt offering in the stead of his son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham lifts up his eyes once more, and “behold behind him a ram caught in a thicket by his horns.” Held by its horns, the animal was unhurt and fit for the altar. Its presence at that place and moment is God’s doing. Abraham asks nothing about where it came from. He recognizes in it the answer to Isaac’s question and to his own words on the hillside: God has provided.

Abraham “went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt offering in the stead of his son.” No further command is recorded; he understands what the ram is for. The wood, the fire, the knife, and the altar were not prepared in vain. The burnt offering God asked for is offered—but the victim is another.

“In the stead of his son” is the first explicit statement in Scripture of one life given in place of another. Substitution had been implied in earlier sacrifices, but here it is spelled out: the ram dies so that Isaac may live. The principle runs through the later sacrificial system, where the worshipper laid his hand on the animal’s head and it was accepted for him (Leviticus 1:4), and through the Passover, when the lamb’s blood sheltered the firstborn (Exodus 12:13). Every firstborn son in Israel would be redeemed by a substitute (Exodus 13:13–15), a standing reminder that the son of promise had been spared by God’s provision.

All these substitutes point beyond themselves to Christ. Isaiah foresaw the Servant on whom the LORD laid “the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6), and Peter declares that Christ “his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). Isaac represents every sinner under sentence of death, bound and helpless on the altar; the ram represents the Substitute whom God Himself supplies. Salvation begins with God, is supplied by God, and is received by the one who trusts Him.

One difference stands out. Isaac had a substitute; Christ had none. When the Son of God came to His altar, no voice from heaven halted the stroke and no ram was found in the thicket. He was Himself the provision, and the mercy shown to Isaac on Moriah was paid for, in the end, at Calvary.

wordNotes.term: תַּחַת בְּנוֹ (tachat beno) — in the stead of his son
wordNotes.explanation: The preposition tachat means under, and by extension in place of or instead of. It describes one person or thing taking the position of another, as Seth was given “instead of Abel” and the Levites were taken “instead of all the firstborn.” Here it states plainly that the ram died in Isaac’s place, the clearest expression of substitution in Genesis.

A mature male sheep, valued in sacrifice and prescribed for burnt offerings, guilt offerings, and the ordination of priests. A ram also served as the burnt offering of the high priest on the Day of Atonement. Isaac had asked about a lamb; God supplied a full-grown ram, more than was expected.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham called the name of that place Jehovah-jireh: as it is said to this day, In the mount of the LORD it shall be seen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham names the place “Jehovah-jireh,” “The LORD will see” or “The LORD will provide.” The name repeats the confession he had made to Isaac (v. 8), now with the covenant name of God. He does not name the mountain after his own obedience. It is remembered for what God did, and the lesson of the chapter is gathered into a single name: the God who commands is also the God who supplies.

The narrator adds a saying current in his own day: “In the mount of the LORD it shall be seen.” The verb is the same, now in a passive form: it shall be seen, or He shall be seen, or it shall be provided. The wordplay holds the meanings together. On this mountain the LORD would provide, and on this mountain the LORD would appear. The saying lived on in Israel as an expression of hope that God would meet His people and supply their need at the place of His choosing.

“The mount of the LORD” became a standard name for Zion, the temple hill in Jerusalem (Psalm 24:3; Isaiah 2:3). There on Moriah Solomon built the house of God, and there the glory of the LORD filled the temple (2 Chronicles 3:1; 7:1–3). Countless lambs were offered on its altar, each one renewing Isaac’s question and Abraham’s answer. Just outside the city that grew around that mount, the Lamb of God was crucified. What had been said “to this day” found its fullest meaning at Golgotha, where God was seen in His Son and provided the sacrifice that ends all others (Hebrews 9:26).

For the believer, Jehovah-jireh is first a confession about the cross: the deepest need of all, a sacrifice for sin, has already been seen to by God. From that gift flows confidence for every other need. Paul could promise the Philippians, “my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:19), because the greater provision had already been made.

wordNotes.term: יְהוָה יִרְאֶה (YHWH yir’eh) — Jehovah-jireh, the LORD will provide
wordNotes.explanation: The name joins the covenant name of God to the verb “he will see.” In context, seeing means seeing to a need and supplying it, as Abraham had confessed in verse 8. The name commemorates God’s act on the mountain and expresses confidence that He will continue to act for His people. It echoes Hagar’s name for the LORD, “Thou God seest me.”

wordNotes.term: בְּהַר יְהוָה יֵרָאֶה (behar YHWH yera’eh) — in the mount of the LORD it shall be seen
wordNotes.explanation: The verb is now passive (niphal), “it will be seen” or “he will appear.” The same form describes the LORD appearing to the patriarchs and His promise to appear in the cloud above the mercy seat. The proverb therefore links provision with God’s self-revelation at the place He chooses for worship.

verses.bibleText: And the angel of the LORD called unto Abraham out of heaven the second time,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
After the ram has been offered, the Angel of the LORD calls “the second time.” The first call stopped the knife; the second confirms the covenant. Coming again from heaven, it ties the oath that follows to the obedience just displayed.

This is the last recorded time God speaks to Abraham. He will live many more years, buy a burial place for Sarah, and arrange Isaac’s marriage, but no further divine speech to him is recorded. The final word he hears from God is a sworn blessing gathering up every promise he had received since Haran. A life that began with a call to go ends, as far as divine speech is concerned, with an assurance that nothing God had promised would fail.

The speaker is again the LORD Himself, as the next verse makes plain. The One who stayed Abraham’s hand is the One who binds Himself by oath, at once the Deliverer of Isaac and the Guarantor of the promise to Abraham’s seed.

wordNotes.explanation: An adverb meaning a second time or again. It marks this call as a distinct sequel to the first in verse 11. The same word introduces the LORD’s second word to Jonah and to Jeremiah, where a repeated message carries renewed assurance.

verses.bibleText: And said, By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD, for because thou hast done this thing, and hast not withheld thy son, thine only son:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD.” This is the first time Scripture records God confirming His promise to Abraham with an oath, and later references to the oath sworn to the fathers look back to this moment (Genesis 26:3; 50:24). People swear by someone greater than themselves, calling on God as witness. Since there is no one greater than God, He swears by Himself (Hebrews 6:13). His own being and character stand behind His word. The formula “saith the LORD,” so frequent in the prophets, is rare in the books of Moses and solemnly marks this utterance as divine.

The oath does not make God’s promise truer than it already was. It is given for the sake of Abraham and his heirs. Hebrews explains that God, “willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel,” confirmed it by an oath, so that those who flee to Him for refuge might have strong consolation (Hebrews 6:17–18). The writer then ties that hope to Christ, who has entered within the veil as forerunner and high priest (Hebrews 6:19–20). The oath of Moriah thus anchors Christian assurance in the heavenly ministry of Christ.

“Because thou hast done this thing, and hast not withheld thy son, thine only son.” The reason is stated twice in the speech (vv. 16 and 18). Abraham’s obedience did not earn the covenant; the promises had been given freely years before, when Abraham had done nothing to deserve them (Genesis 12:1–3; 15:5–6). What the oath confirms is that God’s gracious purpose and Abraham’s answering faith now stand together. Grace called Abraham and carried him through his failures in Egypt and Gerar. On Moriah that grace bore fruit in a faith that obeyed to the uttermost, and God set His seal on it.

wordNotes.term: בִּי נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי (bi nishba‘ti) — by myself have I sworn
wordNotes.explanation: To swear “by” someone is to stake one’s word on that person’s life or honour. God has no one higher to appeal to, so He swears by Himself, pledging His own nature as the guarantee. The few other passages with this expression concern promises or judgments God has fixed beyond reversal.

A solemn formula meaning “utterance of the LORD,” used hundreds of times in the prophets to mark a word as directly from God. Its appearance here gives the Angel’s speech the full weight of a divine oracle and identifies the speaker with the LORD Himself.

verses.bibleText: That in blessing I will bless thee, and in multiplying I will multiply thy seed as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand which is upon the sea shore; and thy seed shall possess the gate of his enemies;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The blessing is stated with intensifying Hebrew constructions: “in blessing I will bless thee, and in multiplying I will multiply.” The doubled verbs express certainty and fullness. What God had promised, He would do completely.

Two images describe Abraham’s descendants. The stars of the heaven recall the night vision of Genesis 15:5; the sand upon the sea shore echoes the dust of the earth in Genesis 13:16. Together they speak of a multitude beyond counting. The New Testament sees that multitude in all who share Abraham’s faith, Jew and Gentile alike (Romans 4:16–18; Galatians 3:29), and Revelation pictures it as a great company that no one could number, from every nation (Revelation 7:9).

“Thy seed shall possess the gate of his enemies” is a new element in the promises. The city gate was the place of defence, government, and judgment; to possess an enemy’s gate meant to overcome and rule his city. In the near view this pointed to Israel’s entry into Canaan and victory over its foes. The Hebrew keeps the singular “seed” with “his enemies,” leaving room for a single representative descendant. That recalls the first promise in Eden, where the woman’s Seed would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). Christ is that conquering Seed. He has triumphed over the powers of darkness at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and His victory will be complete when He returns in glory and the last enemy, death, is destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).

Rebekah’s family would later send her away with nearly the same words: may your seed possess the gate of those who hate them (Genesis 24:60). The echo suggests that the promise spoken on Moriah was known and cherished within the wider family.

wordNotes.term: בָרֵךְ אֲבָרֶכְךָ (barekh avarekhkha) — in blessing I will bless thee
wordNotes.explanation: The infinitive absolute placed before a finite verb of the same root is a Hebrew way of adding emphasis: “I will surely bless you.” The same construction follows with “multiplying I will multiply.” Hebrews 6:14 quotes this line directly from the Greek Old Testament as the content of God’s oath.

wordNotes.term: שַׁעַר אֹיְבָיו (sha‘ar ’oyevaw) — the gate of his enemies
wordNotes.explanation: The gate stood for the strength and authority of a city, where elders sat in judgment and defenders held their ground. To possess the gate was to gain control of the city itself. The singular pronoun “his” keeps the focus on the seed as one, which Paul treats as significant for identifying the promised Seed with Christ.

verses.bibleText: And in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed; because thou hast obeyed my voice.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed.” The promise of Genesis 12:3, first given when Abraham left Haran, is confirmed under oath and now tied explicitly to his seed. From the beginning God’s choice of Abraham was meant to reach beyond Abraham. It was a plan to bring blessing to every nation through one family and, finally, through one Person.

Paul makes the point directly. Scripture, he writes, “preached before the gospel unto Abraham” in this promise (Galatians 3:8), and the seed in view is singular: “And to thy seed, which is Christ” (Galatians 3:16). Peter, preaching in the temple courts on Moriah itself, quoted this promise and announced that God had raised up His Son Jesus to bless his hearers “in turning away every one of you from his iniquities” (Acts 3:25–26). The blessing of the nations is the gospel: forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life through the Seed who was given for the world.

The Hebrew verb can be read “shall be blessed” or “shall bless themselves.” Either way, the nations find blessing by being joined to Abraham’s Seed. The New Testament leaves no doubt that this happens through faith: “they which be of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham” (Galatians 3:9).

“Because thou hast obeyed my voice.” The clause does not turn grace into wages. Abraham’s obedience was the fruit of the faith God had awakened in him, and God delighted to honour it. Later the LORD tells Isaac that the blessing will pass to him “because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws” (Genesis 26:5). In Abraham’s life faith and obedience cannot be pulled apart. The true Seed fulfilled that pattern perfectly: Christ “became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:8), and by His obedience many are made righteous (Romans 5:19).

wordNotes.term: וְהִתְבָּרְכוּ בְזַרְעֲךָ (wehitbarekhu bezar‘akha) — in thy seed shall… be blessed
wordNotes.explanation: The reflexive form of the verb may mean “they will bless themselves” or “they will find blessing” by means of Abraham’s seed. In either sense the nations obtain blessing through their relation to that seed. The Greek Old Testament reads a passive, “shall be blessed,” and this is the form quoted by Peter and Paul in announcing the gospel to Jews and Gentiles.

wordNotes.term: עֵקֶב אֲשֶׁר שָׁמַעְתָּ בְּקֹלִי (‘eqev ’asher shama‘ta beqoli) — because thou hast obeyed my voice
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “as a consequence that you listened to my voice.” In Hebrew, to hear someone’s voice often means to obey. The phrase names Abraham’s obedience as the occasion of the oath and is repeated almost exactly when the promise is confirmed to Isaac, where it is expanded to include God’s commandments, statutes, and laws.

verses.bibleText: So Abraham returned unto his young men, and they rose up and went together to Beer-sheba; and Abraham dwelt at Beer-sheba.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The story ends where it began, with ordinary movement. Abraham returns to the young men, and together they travel home to Beer-sheba. The note that “they rose up and went together” echoes the twice-repeated description of father and son walking “together” (vv. 6, 8). What began as a lonely climb toward death ends as a shared journey home.

Isaac is not named in this verse, and some readers have wondered at the silence. The narrator’s focus stays on Abraham, whose test the chapter records, and Abraham’s promise “we will… come again to you” (v. 5) assumes that Isaac returned. The words he spoke at the foot of the mountain have come true exactly.

Abraham “dwelt at Beer-sheba,” the place where he had planted a grove and called on “the everlasting God” (Genesis 21:33). Life resumes its daily course, and the next chapters tell of a well-ordered household, a burial purchased in faith, and a servant sent to find a bride. The experience on the mountain did not lift Abraham out of ordinary duties; it sent him back to them with a faith that had been tried and found true. Believers who meet God in great trials are meant, like Abraham, to carry what they learned back into the routine of home, work, and worship.

The silence of the closing verse also leaves something unsaid. No emotional reunion is described, no conversation on the road home, no report to Sarah. The narrator has told what God did and what Abraham believed. The rest of Abraham’s life will show how lastingly Moriah shaped him: he never again appears hesitating over God’s promise.

wordNotes.explanation: The name means “well of the oath” or “well of seven,” recalling the covenant with Abimelech sealed by seven ewe lambs. It lay at the southern edge of the land and became the traditional southern limit of Israel. Abraham returns from the place of God’s oath on Moriah to the place named for a human oath.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass after these things, that it was told Abraham, saying, Behold, Milcah, she hath also born children unto thy brother Nahor;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass after these things” repeats the opening words of verse 1 and signals a new section. The first time, those words introduced a command that seemed to end Abraham’s future. Now they introduce news that opens it. A report reaches Beer-sheba from Abraham’s relatives in Mesopotamia: Milcah has borne children to Nahor.

Nahor and Milcah were introduced long before, in the family record of Terah (Genesis 11:29). Milcah was the daughter of Abraham’s brother Haran and had married her uncle Nahor. The little word “also” is suggestive. Sarah had borne a son after long barrenness; Milcah too has become a mother of many. The report implies that years have passed since Abraham last heard from his kin.

Placed immediately after the oath to multiply Abraham’s seed, the news turns attention to the next generation. Isaac has been restored to his father, and he will need a wife from among his own people, not from the Canaanites (Genesis 24:3–4). Far away in Haran, God’s providence was already preparing that answer before Abraham began to seek it.

wordNotes.term: מִלְכָּה גַם־הִוא (Milkah gam-hi’) — Milcah, she hath also
wordNotes.explanation: The emphatic “she also” links Milcah’s motherhood with Sarah’s. Both women belong to Terah’s family, and both have now borne children. The name Milkah is related to the word for queen. Her mention prepares the reader to recognize her granddaughter when Rebekah appears at the well and names her family.

verses.bibleText: Huz his firstborn, and Buz his brother, and Kemuel the father of Aram,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The list begins with Nahor’s firstborn, Huz (Uz), a name that also appears among the sons of Aram (Genesis 10:23) and later as the land where Job lived (Job 1:1). The second son is Buz. A tribe of that name is grouped with Dedan and Tema in Jeremiah 25:23, and Elihu, the young speaker in Job, is called “the Buzite” (Job 32:2).

Kemuel is described as “the father of Aram,” distinguishing this Aram from the son of Shem. The name points ahead: Jacob would later serve in Aram, and Israel would confess at the harvest altar, “A Syrian ready to perish was my father” (Deuteronomy 26:5). The relatives left behind in Mesopotamia remained bound up with the line of promise.

wordNotes.term: אֲבִי אֲרָם (’avi ’Aram) — the father of Aram
wordNotes.explanation: “Father of” in a genealogy can designate the ancestor of a people or the founder of a town or clan. This Aram, grandson of Nahor, is distinct from Aram the son of Shem. The name later identifies the region of Paddan-aram, home of Laban and the scene of Jacob’s exile.

verses.bibleText: And Chesed, and Hazo, and Pildash, and Jidlaph, and Bethuel.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Five more sons complete Milcah’s eight. Chesed may be connected with the Chaldeans (Kasdim), the people of the region from which Abraham’s family had come (Genesis 11:28, 31). Hazo, Pildash, and Jidlaph are otherwise unknown. The list moves briskly until it reaches the name that matters most for the story: Bethuel, the youngest.

Bethuel’s place at the end is significant. Genesis repeatedly shows God working through those who are not first by birth—Seth after Abel, Isaac rather than Ishmael, Jacob rather than Esau. The genealogy draws attention to Bethuel because through him the next mother of the promised line would come (Genesis 24:15).

wordNotes.explanation: The meaning of the name is uncertain; it includes the element ’el, “God.” Bethuel is consistently identified as the son of Nahor and Milcah and the father of Rebekah and Laban, though in Genesis 24 his son Laban takes the leading role in the family’s negotiations.

verses.bibleText: And Bethuel begat Rebekah: these eight Milcah did bear to Nahor, Abraham's brother.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrator pauses within the list: “And Bethuel begat Rebekah.” She is the only granddaughter named and the only member of the following generation mentioned at all. The genealogy exists largely to introduce her. In the next chapters she will become Isaac’s wife, the mother of Jacob and Esau, and a vital link in the chain of promise (Genesis 24:67; 25:20–23).

Rebekah was related to Abraham on both sides of his family: through Nahor, his brother, and through Milcah, the daughter of his brother Haran. Her brother Laban, not yet mentioned here, would later become the father of Leah and Rachel (Genesis 29:16).

The summary “these eight Milcah did bear to Nahor” closes the first part of the list. The placement of the notice right after God’s oath is no accident. The God who has just sworn to bless the nations through Abraham’s seed is already preparing the bride through whom that seed will continue. Providence runs ahead of human plans, often unnoticed, as Abraham’s servant would discover at the well when he blessed the LORD for leading him “to the house of my master’s brethren” (Genesis 24:27).

wordNotes.explanation: The meaning of the name is uncertain. Rebekah is the only daughter named in Nahor’s genealogy, which marks her as its purpose. She will show hospitality and decisive faith in leaving her home for Isaac, and Paul later recalls her as the mother through whom God’s electing purpose was revealed before her twins were born.

verses.bibleText: And his concubine, whose name was Reumah, she bare also Tebah, and Gaham, and Thahash, and Maachah.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Nahor also had four sons by his concubine Reumah: Tebah, Gaham, Thahash, and Maachah. A concubine was a secondary wife, and her children held a lesser place in the inheritance. Little is known of these sons, though the name Maachah later belongs to an Aramean kingdom near Mount Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:14; 2 Samuel 10:6).

The total of twelve sons—eight by the principal wife and four by the secondary wife—matches the twelve princes of Ishmael (Genesis 25:13–16) and the twelve sons of Jacob, eight by Leah and Rachel and four by their maids (Genesis 35:22–26). The pattern suggests God’s ordering hand over the whole family of Terah. Yet only one line carries the covenant promise, and the genealogy has already pointed to it in Rebekah.

wordNotes.explanation: Pilegesh denotes a wife of secondary rank, often without the full rights of the principal wife and whose sons might receive gifts in place of an equal inheritance. Abraham’s sons by his concubines were treated this way. The word is applied to Keturah and to Bilhah in the patriarchal narratives.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What would it mean to trust God with the very thing through which He has promised to bless you?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God tested Abraham’s faith to its limit, and on Moriah He revealed Himself as the God who provides the substitute, pointing to the gift of His own Son.
discussionQuestions: Why does the narrator tell the reader in verse 1 that this is a test, while Abraham is not told?
How do Abraham’s words in verses 5 and 8 reveal what he believed about God’s promise?
In what ways do Isaac and the ram each point to Christ, and where does the comparison break down?
How do Hebrews 11:17-19 and James 2:21-23 together explain the relation between Abraham’s faith and his obedience?
What does the name Jehovah-jireh teach about where our confidence should rest in times of testing?
commonMisunderstandings: The chapter does not show that God desires human sacrifice; it shows God forbidding it and supplying a substitute.
God’s “now I know” does not mean God lacked knowledge; it means Abraham’s faith was displayed in history.
Abraham’s obedience did not earn the covenant, which God had given freely long before; it revealed a faith God had formed.
Divine testing is not temptation to sin; God proves His servants in order to strengthen and bless them.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the focus on what God provides. Abraham’s obedience is real and exemplary, but the mountain is named for the LORD’s provision, which reaches its fulfilment in the sacrifice of Christ.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Bring to God whatever you are tempted to hold back from Him, and trust the One who did not withhold His own Son to see to every need that follows.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God Himself provides the substitute: Christ, the Lamb of God, dies in the sinner’s place so that all who believe may live.
flow: Like Isaac on the altar, every person stands under the sentence of death that sin brings.
No human effort can supply the sacrifice that sin requires; Isaac’s question “where is the lamb?” has no human answer.
God provided a ram in Isaac’s stead, a picture of the substitute He would give.
At Calvary, near Moriah, the Father gave His only Son, and no substitute was found for Him because He was the substitute.
Those who trust Christ receive life as a gift and respond with the obedient faith Abraham displayed.
simpleIllustrations: A condemned prisoner is freed when another willingly takes his place; the freed man owes his life to the one who died.
A father who gives what he loves most for someone else shows the measure of his love more clearly than any words.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you receive the Lamb God has provided and trust Him with your life and future?
cautions: Do not present the story as though God were cruel or arbitrary; the reader is told at the outset that it is a test, and God forbids the sacrifice.
Do not reduce Jehovah-jireh to a promise of material prosperity; its first meaning is God’s provision of a sacrifice for sin.
Do not imply that obedience purchases salvation; Abraham’s obedience flowed from faith in a God who had already promised freely.

reflectionQuestions: Is there a gift from God that I am holding more tightly than I hold the Giver?
When God’s command and my understanding of His promise seem to conflict, do I trust Him enough to keep walking?
How does the thought that the Father did not withhold His Son change the way I face my own losses?
Where have I seen the LORD provide in ways I could not have arranged myself?
What did I learn in a past trial that I need to carry back into ordinary life today?
